item.title: Gloria Steinem: A life in pictures
item.description:
For years, when interviewers asked for a favorite quote, I gave them Gloria Steinem’s: “We are linked, not ranked.” She used the line in 2013 as shorthand for her whole political vision. Women are not a tournament. We are not climbing over one another toward a single chair. We thrive when we treat our connection as a circle instead of a hierarchy. I needed that line. In corporate life in the 1990s and early 2000s, the conventional wisdom held that there was room for only a few of us in executive team rooms and that the smart play was to swat the woman next to you out of the way. Steinem’s sentence rejected that scarcity story. The problem was the ranking, not the other woman. I am a feminist. I adopted the word in college. Before that I was an athlete training eight hours a day, with no political opinions to speak of. What I had was a body that coaches treated as theirs to break and use…

item.title: Gloria Steinem Stayed Positive, Even as the Manosphere Took Hold
item.description:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. T hroughout most of Gloria Steinem’s life , two versions of her existed. Publicly, Steinem was a figurehead: the glamorous co-founder of Ms. magazine, a totem for second-wave feminism and a bull’s-eye for its detractors, gorgeously inscrutable behind her curtains of streaked hair and tinted glasses. Privately, she was a workhorse: someone who hid behind her accessories, felt she’d come to the women’s movement late (in her mid-30s), and spent much of the rest of her life hustling to make up for it. If these two identities came into conflict—the persona and the person, the superstar feminist who was terrified of public speaking—Steinem, who died yesterday at the age of 92, simply pushed on. Her politics and her life both revolved around her steadfast commitment to the idea that all women are human…

item.title: Opinion: The One Stereotype That Gloria Steinem Shockingly Busted
item.description:
Janet Fries / Getty Images The old joke “How many feminists does it take to screw in a light bulb?” has no punchline. Instead, the joke teller waits for the other person to offer a response, then jumps in angrily to say, “That’s not funny!” Of all the stereotypes that Gloria Steinem destroyed, my favorite was that feminists don’t have a sense of humor. Gloria was funny. How funny was she? She was funny enough that she received an Emmy nomination for being on the writing staff of the 1965 satirical news show, That Was the Week That Was, where her fellow writers included Buck Henry ( Get Smart, The Graduate ), Herb Sargent ( SNL Weekend Update ), and Thomas Meehan (book for the musical The Producers ).
